Executive Summary — Where Is Institutional Money Flowing?

Two lenses on the same question — where did money move this week, and across which markets (US, India, Global, Commodity)?

5.1 — Global: Macros, Commodities, US Stocks, US & Global ETFs

The big picture — Global
A single geopolitical shock — renewed US-Iran military strikes on 1 September — cascaded through nearly every global asset class this week, and the dominant flow was into safety, not out of it uniformly. Oil spiked (Brent +5% in a day, holding $95-97/bbl), which combined with hawkish Fed commentary to drive a global bond selloff (US 10Y broke above 4.80%, highest since Jan 2025). That yield spike hit gold hard mid-week (-2.86% Tuesday) before a dovish pivot from Fed Governor Waller reversed both the yield move and gold's slide by Friday. US equities felt this most acutely: only 466 of 957 stocks (49%) were positive — better than last week's 40% but still soft — while the broader US ETF universe was almost exactly split (2,148 of 4,332 advancing, 49.6%), suggesting broad indecision rather than a clear rotation.

Global ETFs told a more constructive story than US stocks: 29 of 47 country/region ETFs were positive, led by Brazil (+6.50%) and a cluster of Asia-Pacific markets (South Korea +4.81%, Taiwan +3.97%, Indonesia +3.16%). The weakest were concentrated in commodity-linked and Middle East names — Sprott Critical Materials (-5.69%), Copper Miners (-3.98% and -2.60%), and Saudi Arabia (-1.91%) — consistent with the mid-week commodity selloff before the late-week rebound. Latin America (+3.01% average) and Asia-Pacific (+1.39% average) were the strongest regions; North America (-1.22%) and Commodity-linked ETFs (-1.29%) were the weakest.

Read together: this looks like money rotating within risk assets rather than fleeing them wholesale — out of commodity/metals exposure and US mega-cap-heavy indices, into select EM/Asia-Pacific and Latin American markets, with gold's mid-week crash and late-week recovery acting as the clearest single barometer of how fast Fed-hike expectations swung (40%→68%→50% across the week) in response to the unfolding Iran conflict.

5.2 — India: Macros, Indices, Sectors, Stocks

The big picture — India
India had its worst week in this report's history by nearly every measure — even as DII buying hit a third consecutive record. Nifty 50 fell 1.15% (its steepest weekly drop tracked so far, following three prior weeks of milder declines), and breadth turned sharply negative (681 Adv/918 Dec, worse than last week's 740/848). DMA-based breadth confirmed the deterioration: DMA50 crossovers were decisively negative (97 above vs 125 below, net -28, the worst reading yet), and DMA200 crossovers were similarly weak (30 above vs 70 below, net -40). Yet DII bought a record +₹23,156 Cr — domestic conviction has, if anything, strengthened as the index has weakened.

The macro backdrop explains much of this: India's 10Y G-Sec briefly breached 7% intraday (near 3-month high) as the Iran-driven oil spike and global bond selloff hit Indian debt directly, narrowing India's yield advantage over the US and coinciding with the heaviest single-day FII selling in this report's history (-₹7,986 Cr, Monday). Relief arrived mid-week via an unexpected $127 billion FCNR(B) foreign-currency inflow, which eased bond yields and strengthened the rupee (-1.01% vs USD) even as global risk sentiment stayed fragile — a genuinely India-specific positive story cutting against an otherwise negative global backdrop.

At the sector and stock level, the damage was broad rather than concentrated in any one pocket — see Section 05 (India Stocks & Indices tab) for the full sector table. The 52-week-high list shrank for the first time in this report's history (161→143 names), and even the previously-resilient Large Cap DMA50 breadth fell sharply (60.0%→43.0%) — a signal that even the market's most liquid, institutionally-favored names weren't spared this week.

Read together: India this week was "DII record buying, everything else negative" — the most one-sided divergence between domestic conviction and actual price action seen in this report. Worth watching whether DII's buying pace can keep absorbing both FII outflows and a genuinely deteriorating technical picture, or whether a week like this eventually tests that resolve.

Net read — where did the money move this week?
Out of: Indian equities broadly (worst week yet, heaviest single-day FII selling on record), commodity/metals-linked ETFs, and — mid-week — gold and silver on the yield spike. Into: India via DII (a third consecutive record week, +₹23,156 Cr), the rupee (via FCNR inflows, not equity flows), select Asia-Pacific and Latin American equity markets, and gold again by Friday as the Fed's tone turned dovish. The connective tissue: a single geopolitical shock (Iran conflict escalation) drove oil and yields up together, which hit richly-valued and rate-sensitive assets (US mega-caps, gold, Indian bonds and equities) hardest, while a India-specific liquidity event (FCNR inflows) and a late-week dovish Fed pivot both worked to partially offset the damage by Friday.
01

FII / DII Cashflows

🔍 Analyst Take
DII's third consecutive record week (+₹23,156 Cr) against FII's third straight sell week (-₹5,613 Cr) is now a structural pattern, not a blip — cumulative FII flow since 30-Jul has flipped negative for the first time. Watch, don't chase: this kind of DII-absorbs-everything dynamic has historically preceded either (a) a durable floor once FII selling exhausts itself, or (b) a sharper correction if DII pace ever falters. With Monday's -₹7,986 Cr the heaviest single-day FII sell on record here, the read is constructive for large-cap quality names DIIs typically concentrate in (financials, staples) if this is capitulation-stage selling — but risky to over-extend on beta if FII outflows continue and DII buying is merely absorbing supply rather than expressing fresh conviction. Not investment advice — a flows lens, not a valuation one.

02

FX Market — USD/INR

🔍 Analyst Take
The rupee's 3rd straight weekly gain is liquidity-driven (FCNR inflows), not equity-flow-driven — a distinction that matters for durability. FCNR deposits carry maturities and eventual repatriation; this is a temporary tailwind, not a fundamental re-rating of the rupee. Exporters (IT services, pharma) face a modest near-term margin headwind if strength persists into earnings season; import-heavy, dollar-cost-sensitive sectors (oil marketing, aviation) get modest relief. The yen's simultaneous gain against the rupee is the more telling signal — genuine safe-haven demand still favors JPY over INR when the shock is global (Iran conflict) rather than India-specific.

Rupee context
A major driver: the RBI's FCNR(B) deposit scheme attracted over $127 billion in foreign-currency inflows (against ~$90 billion expected), pushing total recent inflows including ECBs and overseas borrowings to $136.38 billion. This boosted banking-system liquidity and directly supported the rupee, even as the broader macro backdrop (Iran conflict, oil spike, global bond selloff) would typically favor safe-haven currencies like the dollar and yen over EM currencies. The yen's gain against the rupee this week reflects that same risk-off dynamic playing out more conventionally elsewhere.
03

Commodities — Weekly Snapshot

🔍 Analyst Take
The gold/silver crash-then-recover pattern this week (Tue -2.86%, recovered by Fri on Waller's dovish pivot) is a textbook Fed-expectations trade, not a change in the structural gold bull case (central bank buying, de-dollarization demand remain intact per multiple sources this week). Dips toward $4,300-4,350 on hawkish Fed repricing look like tactical entry zones for gold-linked exposure if you believe the structural case holds, given three straight sessions of "sell the hike-odds-spike, buy the pivot" behavior. Oil is the bigger open risk: Brent holding $95-97/bbl on an active, unresolved Iran conflict means energy-sensitive Indian sectors (aviation, paints, tyres) carry event risk that a single week of price action won't resolve — this is a geopolitical tail risk, not a seasonal spike.

The oil-yields-gold chain this week
This week is a clean example of a single geopolitical shock (renewed Iran strikes) cascading through multiple asset classes: oil spiked on supply-risk premium → that plus hawkish Fed commentary drove a global bond selloff (US 10Y broke 4.80%, its highest since Jan 2025) → higher real yields raised the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold, crashing it mid-week → then a dovish pivot from Fed Governor Waller reversed the yield move and gold recovered. Fed rate-hike odds for the 15-16 Sept meeting swung from ~40% to ~68% (post-Warsh) back down to ~50% (post-Waller) within the same week — unusually volatile positioning for a single FOMC meeting.
04

Debt Market

🔍 Analyst Take
India's 10Y briefly breaching 7% then retreating to ~6.94% on the FCNR inflow news is a volatility signal worth monitoring, not yet a trend break — the move was event-driven (Iran shock + one-off inflow) on both sides rather than a repricing of India's structural rate path. Rate-sensitive sectors (real estate, NBFCs, auto financing) likely saw the FII selling concentrate here given the yield spike's timing lines up with Monday's record FII outflow. If yields stabilize below 7% next week, this pullback in rate-sensitive names may prove a better entry than the price action alone suggests — but confirm the RBI's tone doesn't turn genuinely hawkish before reading it that way.

What moved yields
India's 10Y briefly breached 7% intraday (1 Sep) — a near 3-month high — on the combination of surging oil (Iran conflict), higher US Treasury yields, and a global debt selloff. This narrowed India's usual yield advantage over the US sharply, raising foreign-outflow risk (consistent with this week's heavy FII selling in Section 1). Relief came mid-week: the RBI's FCNR(B) scheme attracted $127 billion in inflows, boosting liquidity and easing yields back to ~6.94% by Wednesday. On the US side, Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish tone pushed rate-hike odds for the 15-16 Sept FOMC meeting as high as 68% before Fed Governor Waller's more dovish remarks pulled that back to ~50% by Friday — an unusually wide swing in Fed expectations within a single week.

Executive Summary — India Story

Executive Summary — India Story
India's worst week in this report's history, across nearly every measure tracked. Nifty 50 fell 1.15% — the steepest weekly drop tracked so far — and breadth turned sharply negative (681 Adv/918 Dec, worse than last week's 740/848). The 52-week-high list shrank for the first time in this report's history (161→143 names), and DMA-based breadth confirmed broad deterioration: DMA50 crossovers were the worst yet (97 above vs 125 below, net -28), while even Large Cap DMA50 breadth — previously the most resilient bucket — collapsed from 60.0% to 43.0%, the sharpest single-week move for any cap bucket tracked so far. Sector performance was broadly negative rather than concentrated in any one pocket (see the Equity Returns tab for the full breakdown). The top-performers list remains dominated by small, illiquid, largely single-stock/news-driven names rather than a coherent theme, while the bottom-performers and 52-week-high lists both point to genuine, broad-based weakness this week rather than a narrow correction.
01

Equity Returns — Broad & Sector Indices

🔍 Analyst Take
A fourth straight down week, and the sharpest one, breaks the "decelerating decline" pattern that looked reassuring through mid-August. Avoid chasing dip-buys in the weakest sector table entries this week until breadth (Market Breadth tab) confirms stabilization rather than one green day. Sectors holding up relatively better this week are the more credible near-term relative-strength candidates than broad-index bets — check the sector table above for this week's leaders vs laggards before rotating. Given the driver is a global geopolitical shock (not an India-specific earnings or policy issue), a sharp snap-back is plausible if the Iran conflict shows any de-escalation signal — but timing that catalyst is speculation, not analysis.

52-Week High / Near-High Candidates — India

🔍 Analyst Take
This is the first week the 52-week-high list has shrunk (161→143) — a meaningful signal in a market this broadly weak. Names still on this list despite the week's selloff show genuine relative strength and are worth prioritizing over names that just fell off it. Large, liquid names holding within 5% of their high through a week like this (check the Cap Bucket and MCap columns for the biggest, most liquid entries) are the closest thing to a "quality holding up" signal this report can offer. Conversely, any name that dropped off this list versus last week's 161 names is now showing a trend crack worth monitoring, even if it's not yet in the bottom performers.

Market Breadth by Market Cap — DMA 50 / DMA 200

🔍 Analyst Take
Large Cap DMA50 breadth collapsing from 60% to 43% in a single week is the standout signal here — large-cap momentum has broken meaningfully, and this is not a "rotate down the cap curve" market right now given every bucket weakened together. The DMA200-crossed-below list (Section 4.3) is your closest thing to a structured watch-list: names dropping below their 200-day average after holding above it are showing the clearest technical deterioration and warrant a fresh look at the underlying thesis. Conversely, the handful of names that crossed above DMA50 or DMA200 this week did so against a strongly negative tape — that's a higher-conviction signal than a similar cross would be in a strong week, since it happened despite broad selling pressure.
Legend
Cap Bucket: Large = rank 1-100, Mid = 101-250, Small = 251-500, Micro = 501+ (re-ranked fresh each week by mcap). Breadth = % of stocks in that bucket trading above their 50-day / 200-day moving average.

Reading it
Large Cap DMA50 breadth collapsed from 60.0% to 43.0% — the sharpest single-week move for any bucket in this report's history — meaning the market's biggest, most liquid names weren't a safe harbor this week. Mid Cap DMA50 also fell hard (53.3%→46.0%). DMA200 breadth held up somewhat better across all buckets, suggesting this is primarily a short-term momentum shock rather than a longer-term trend break — for now.

Net effect
DMA200: 30 crossed above vs 70 below (net -40, the worst reading yet). DMA50: 97 crossed above vs 125 below (net -28). Both confirm this week's broad deterioration story from 4.1 — a genuinely weak week across the board, not concentrated in any one cap bucket.
CMP

4-Week Comparison — India Stocks (mcap > ₹1,000 Cr)

🔍 Analyst Take
Consistent 4-week gainers worth a closer look: Kotak Mahindra Bank and DLF (both Large Cap, positive every week despite the broader large-cap breakdown noted in the Breadth tab) stand out as genuine relative-strength names, not momentum flukes — a large-cap holding up through four straight weak weeks for the index is a stronger signal than a small-cap doing the same. New India Assurance (+23.4% this week alone, positive all 4 weeks) and Welspun Corp are the more speculative but still-consistent mid-cap entries.

Consistent 4-week laggards — the notable one is who's on this list: HDFC Bank, SBI, Hindustan Unilever, Maruti Suzuki, M&M, ITC, Nestlé India, Asian Paints — this is a cluster of blue-chip, index-heavyweight names underperforming for a full month, not a random sample. That concentration in exactly the names FIIs are most overweight is consistent with the FII-selling story in the Macros tab — worth distinguishing "quality on sale" from "further to fall" here based on your own view of whether FII selling is near exhaustion.

Executive Summary — US Story

Executive Summary — US Story
A genuinely undecided week for US assets, whipsawed by conflicting Fed signals layered on top of the Iran-driven oil/yield shock. US stocks were almost exactly split — 466 of 957 (49%) positive — an improvement on last week's 40% but still soft. The broader US ETF universe (4,332 funds) was similarly split (2,148 positive, 49.6%), suggesting indecision rather than a clear rotation into or out of any theme. The week's volatility is visible in fundamentals too: this week's top gainers include names with extreme growth metrics (e.g. NI growth over 3,000% YoY for one top performer) alongside more modest, steady movers — a reminder that this week's biggest % gainers were often small, volatile names rather than a broad quality rally. See the Top Performers tabs below for the full stock- and ETF-level detail, including PE Ratio and 52-week-high distance for context on valuation and positioning.

Top Performers — US Stocks

🔍 Analyst Take
Median return of -0.11% across 957 stocks confirms a genuinely directionless week — this is not a market giving clear buy or sell signals at the index level. Where it does get clearer: Electrical Equipment & Parts, Capital Markets and Computer Hardware led (+6-7.5% avg), while Travel Services, Software-Application and Internet Retail lagged (-3.8% to -6.0% avg) — a fairly classic "rates up, travel/software multiples compress" pattern given the week's yield spike. The higher median PE among this week's top-50 gainers (28.9x vs 23.8x market-wide) means chasing this week's biggest % movers means paying up for already-elevated multiples — more selective, fundamentals-driven picks from the Weekly Comparison tab's consistent-performer list are a more defensible starting point than this week's raw leaderboard.

Top Performers — US ETFs

🔍 Analyst Take
Fixed Income was the only negative asset class on average (-0.45%) — a direct, mechanical consequence of the week's global bond selloff, not a fund-specific issue; bond ETF weakness here should reverse if yields ease next week, it's not a credit or structural concern. Digital Assets ETFs' outlier strength (+7.10% avg) reflects crypto's own volatility more than a broad risk-on signal — treat this category's gains as high-beta noise, not a trend to extrapolate. The more durable signal is Commodity (+1.62%) and Energy (+1.97%) categories leading, directly tracking the oil/gold story in the Macros tab — this is where the week's fundamental (not just technical) strength actually sits, worth distinguishing from the ETF-level top-50 gainer list, which will be dominated by smaller, more volatile single-theme funds.

A close-to-even week for US assets
Both US stocks (466 of 957, 49%) and US ETFs (2,148 of 4,332, 49.6%) were almost exactly split between advancers and decliners — a market genuinely undecided, reflecting the week's whipsaw between hawkish (Warsh) and dovish (Waller) Fed commentary layered on top of the Iran-driven oil/yield shock.
CMP

4-Week Comparison — US Stocks

🔍 Analyst Take
Consistent 4-week gainers cluster almost entirely in energy/refining: HF Sinclair (DINO), Marathon Petroleum (MPC), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX), Cheniere Energy (LNG), Antero Resources (AR), Halliburton (HAL) — all positive every week, all carrying single-digit-to-teens PE ratios (10-21x). This is about as clean a sector-momentum-plus-reasonable-valuation setup as this report has flagged — the fundamental case (sustained oil/gas strength on the Iran conflict) and the technical case (4-week consistency) are aligned here, though obviously contingent on the geopolitical situation not reversing sharply.

Consistent 4-week laggards are concentrated in travel/leisure: Booking Holdings, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Texas Roadhouse — all negative every week, most at moderate-to-high PE (16-30x). This looks like a genuine consumer-discretionary/travel-demand concern layered on top of the rate-sensitivity story, not just noise — four straight weeks of underperformance across an entire sub-sector is a pattern worth taking seriously rather than a value trap to buy into prematurely.

Executive Summary — Global Story

Executive Summary — Global Story
A recovery week for Global ETFs — 29 of 47 positive, up from last week's 19 — with Latin America and Asia-Pacific leading and commodity/metals-linked names lagging. Brazil (+6.50%) was the standout, more than 1.5x the next-best performer; South Korea, Taiwan, Poland and Indonesia rounded out the top 5. The weakest were concentrated in commodity/metals and Middle East names — consistent with the mid-week gold/silver/copper selloff detailed in the Macros tab. Latin America (+3.01% average) and Asia-Pacific (+1.39% average) were the strongest regions; North America (-1.22%) and Commodity-linked ETFs (-1.29%) were the weakest. Across the two weeks now tracked, 11 of 47 ETFs have been positive both weeks — see the Weekly Comparison tab for the full list and a searchable table.
01

Global ETF Heatmap — Weekly Analysis

🔍 Analyst Take
Latin America and Asia-Pacific leading (+3.0% and +1.4% avg) while Commodity-linked ETFs lag (-1.3% avg) is a notable divergence from the Macros tab's oil/gold strength narrative — country/region ETF performance and commodity-specific fund performance decoupled this week, likely because Brazil's gain (+6.5%) is equity-market-driven (its own domestic story) rather than a pure commodity pass-through. Brazil, South Korea and Taiwan showing the clearest, largest gains are the region-level entries best supported by this week's data — though a single week of outperformance isn't a trend on its own; check the Weekly Comparison tab for which of these have been consistent. Copper and critical-materials-focused ETFs being the worst performers despite copper's earlier-week strength suggests late-week profit-taking in that specific trade — worth distinguishing from a genuine change in the metals thesis.

Weekly Comparison — Global ETFs

🔍 Analyst Take
With only 2 weeks tracked, 11 of 47 ETFs positive both weeks is a small enough sample that this list should be treated as "worth watching for a 3rd confirming week," not yet an actionable signal. That said, the composition is informative: Brazil, South Korea and Taiwan being both this week's biggest gainers and on the 2-week-consistent list is a stronger combination than either fact alone — these three deserve priority attention once a 3rd or 4th week of data confirms the pattern. The S&P 500 and Belgium ETFs appearing on this list with only marginal gains (+0.11%, +0.05%) are more "avoided a down week" than "showing real strength" — worth distinguishing from the more decisively positive names above them.
